[STAMP’s author implementation](https://github.com/uestcnlp/STAMP/blob/master/model/STAMP_rsc.py) combines mean session memory m̄ with latest-item embedding e_t: α_i=vᵀσ(W₁e_i+W₂e_t+W₃m̄+b), a=Σ_iα_i e_i, and f=tanh(U(a+m̄))⊙tanh(Ve_t). Latest-item conditioning therefore affects both attention and multiplicative readout. [NARM](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.04725) instead uses GRU states: α_ti=vᵀσ(A₁h_t+A₂h_i), c=[h_t;Σ_iα_ti h_i], score(j)=e_jᵀBc. Its query h_t summarizes the prefix, rather than exposing only e_t. Both models’ longer context is within-session.

[HRM](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/classes/fa17/cse291-b/reading/SIGIR2015_NextBasketRec.pdf) predicts from f₂(u,f₁({e_i:i∈last basket})), combining a learned user vector with pooled latest-basket items; it does not recurrently encode earlier baskets. Its four average/max-pooling variants favor max/max. NARM’s hybrid encoder beats either component alone: DIGINETICA Recall@20 at dimension 100 is 62.58 versus 61.88 global-only and 61.71 attentive-only. These support complementary representations, not identification of intent. STAMP’s original ablation tables could not be verified from accessible primary material.

The proposed GRU4Rec readout f_t=(1−g_t)h_t+g_tWe_t is an additive scalar-gated latest-item bypass, conceptually related to these established combinations, though algebraically distinct. With dot-product scoring, its bypass directly supplies a learned item-to-item transition score. Proposed controls: separately retrain g=0, g=1, fixed-gate and learned-gate variants; truncate history to the last item; shuffle earlier history while preserving the last item; evaluate histories sharing that item and stratify by training transition frequency. Gains over last-item-only controls, plus sensitivity to relevant earlier context, support useful conditioning. Gate values, attention plots, or aggregate HR gains alone establish neither history use nor intent alignment.
